title: Universal Basic Income
description: Four extracts from a public debate on whether every citizen should receive a regular, unconditional payment.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · The case for
parts.intro: You will hear the chair, Peter, introducing the debate, followed by the first speaker, Dr Salazar.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Good evening and welcome to tonight's debate. The motion before us is that every adult citizen should receive a regular payment from the state, with no conditions attached. We will hear first from Dr Salazar, who is speaking in favour. You have six minutes, Doctor.

script.speaker: Dr Salazar
script.text: Thank you. I want to begin with a simple observation. Our welfare system was designed for a world of steady jobs and stable families, and it has become a maze. People must prove they are poor, prove they are looking for work and prove, repeatedly, that nothing has changed. Each of those checks costs money, and each is a trap, because the moment you earn a little extra you may lose more in benefits than you gain.

script.speaker: Dr Salazar
script.text: A basic income removes the trap. Everybody receives the same sum, whether they work or not, and every pound you earn is yours to keep on top of it. The incentive to take a small job, or to start a small business, is restored. Critics assume that people given money will stop working. Yet the experience of those who have tried it suggests that most people use security to take more risks, not fewer.

script.speaker: Dr Salazar
script.text: There is also a deeper argument, and it concerns dignity. At present, the system treats the poor as suspects. A universal payment treats everyone as a citizen with a share in the wealth that society produces together. And as automation changes the nature of work, I believe we will need that principle more, not less.

script.speaker: Dr Salazar
script.text: I will not claim that it is cheap. It is not. But I would ask the audience to compare it with the hidden costs we already pay, in ill health, in lost talent and in the sheer bureaucracy of means testing. I submit that a society which can afford to bail out its banks can afford to guarantee its people a floor.

parts.title: Part 2 · The case against
parts.intro: You will hear the opposing speaker, Mr Okonkwo, replying to the motion.

script.speaker: Mr Okonkwo
script.text: I am grateful to my opponent, who has spoken eloquently, and I share her frustration with the present system. But frustration with a bad machine is not an argument for building a bigger one. The question tonight is not whether welfare needs reform. It is whether this particular reform is wise, and I say that it is not.

script.speaker: Mr Okonkwo
script.text: Let us start with arithmetic. If you give every adult a payment large enough to live on, the cost is staggering, many times what we spend on benefits now. There are only two ways to pay for it. You can raise taxes dramatically, or you can set the payment so low that it replaces nothing. Neither, I submit, delivers the promised revolution.

script.speaker: Mr Okonkwo
script.text: A lower payment is not harmless, either. If it is paid in place of targeted support, then the disabled, the chronically ill and single parents, who need far more than the average person, could be left worse off. Money handed to a wealthy citizen is money not available to those in desperate need. Universality sounds fair, but it is blind to difference.

script.speaker: Mr Okonkwo
script.text: My third objection is less about economics and more about values. Work gives people more than a wage. It provides structure, belonging and a sense of contribution. I am not suggesting that everyone would stop working. I am saying that a society which pays people regardless of what they give may slowly forget why contribution matters.

script.speaker: Mr Okonkwo
script.text: I would rather spend that money on training, on childcare and on decent jobs. That is a harder path, I admit, and a less glamorous one. But it respects people as participants rather than recipients.

parts.title: Part 3 · An economist weighs the evidence
parts.intro: You will hear an economist, Professor Lindqvist, commenting on trials of basic income.

script.speaker: Professor Lindqvist
script.text: Since both speakers appealed to evidence, let me say what the trials actually show, which is rather less than either would like. Over the past decade, governments and charities have run small experiments in several countries. The typical design gives a few hundred people a modest monthly sum for a year or two and compares them with a similar group who receive nothing.

script.speaker: Professor Lindqvist
script.text: On the question of laziness, the results are fairly reassuring. Recipients did not generally stop working, although some reduced their hours slightly, and those who did often used the time for study or care of relatives. Wellbeing improved, with lower stress and better mental health. These are real gains, and I would not dismiss them.

script.speaker: Professor Lindqvist
script.text: However, I must add three cautions. First, the payments were temporary. People behave differently when they know the money will stop, so we cannot assume the same response to a permanent guarantee. Second, the samples were small and often confined to one town, which says nothing about the effect on a whole economy, such as the price of housing. Third, because nobody pays for the trial with higher taxes, we learn little about how taxpayers would react.

script.speaker: Professor Lindqvist
script.text: So, in my reading, the trials rebut the crudest fear, that people will simply stop working, but they cannot settle the central question of affordability. Anyone who says the evidence proves their case, on either side, is claiming more than it will bear.

parts.title: Part 4 · Questions and closing
parts.intro: You will hear a member of the audience, Mai, asking a question, and the chair, Peter, responding.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: My question is for the speaker in favour. You say the payment would be freely given, but who exactly pays? A nurse who works nights would be taxed to fund a person who chooses to surf all day. Is that fair?

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: I will let the speaker answer, but may I remind the audience that the question has been put with some feeling.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I mean it sincerely, Chair. I'm not trying to be provocative. I work with people on low pay every day, and many of them feel that nobody on either side of politics is thinking about them. I simply want to know whether this idea would give them anything real, or whether it would merely sound generous on a platform like this one.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Quite so. Dr Salazar, if you would.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: And to be clear, I'm actually undecided. I would like to be persuaded, but so far I have heard a great many principles and rather few figures, and I am wary of anything that sounds too good to be true.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Then let us hear the answer, and then I will ask both speakers to sum up in one minute each. Remember that this audience will vote before it leaves, and I would invite you to vote on the argument, not on the speaker.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Thank you. I think what troubles me most is the idea that something so large could be decided on the strength of small experiments.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: That, if I may say so, is a point on which the speakers and the economist seemed to agree. Let us see whether the closing statements can move you. After that, the ballot papers will be handed out at the door.

questions.text: What is the motion being debated?
options: That banks should pay more tax to fund welfare
That every adult should receive an unconditional state payment
That welfare should be abolished for working adults
That wages should be raised for the lowest paid
questions.explanation: The chair says every adult citizen should receive a regular payment with no conditions.

evidence.quote: every adult citizen should receive a regular payment from the state, with no conditions attached

questions.text: What problem with the current system does Dr Salazar describe?
options: Benefits are too generous for people who work
Jobs are too stable to need any support
Applications are impossible to find or complete online
Earning a little extra can leave people worse off
questions.explanation: She says that earning extra may lose more in benefits than is gained.

evidence.quote: you may lose more in benefits than you gain

questions.text: Why does she say a basic income would restore incentives?
options: The payment is conditional on finding some work
Earnings are kept on top of the payment
Employers have to pay much higher wages
The payment is taxed heavily at higher incomes
questions.explanation: Because every pound earned is kept on top of the payment.

evidence.quote: every pound you earn is yours to keep on top of it

questions.text: What does Dr Salazar say about the idea of dignity?
options: The poor should accept less in return for security
Dignity is not really a political issue at all
The current system treats the poor as suspects
Citizens should repay the state when they can
questions.explanation: She says the system treats the poor as suspects, whereas a universal payment treats everyone as a citizen.

evidence.quote: the system treats the poor as suspects

questions.text: Why does she mention the bailing out of banks?
options: To blame the banks for causing unemployment today
To argue that society can afford a guaranteed floor
To suggest cutting bank profits to pay for it
To prove that the policy is cheap to run
questions.explanation: She says a society that can bail out banks can afford to guarantee a floor.

evidence.quote: can afford to guarantee its people a floor

questions.text: How does Mr Okonkwo begin his reply?
options: By agreeing that the present system is frustrating
By rejecting every point that she had made
By asking the chair for some more time
By praising the motion before attacking it
questions.explanation: He shares her frustration with the present system but says that is no reason for this reform.

evidence.quote: I share her frustration with the present system

questions.text: What are the two ways of paying for a large payment, according to him?
options: Cutting defence spending or selling off public property
Raising taxes dramatically or setting the payment very low
Charging employers or students much higher fees
Printing more money or borrowing from other countries
questions.explanation: He says you either raise taxes dramatically or set the payment so low that it replaces nothing.

evidence.quote: You can raise taxes dramatically, or you can set the payment so low that it replaces nothing.

questions.text: Why might a lower universal payment harm some people?
options: Wealthy citizens would refuse to accept it
Those with greater needs could lose targeted support
Employers would reduce wages to compensate
Everyone would receive less than they did before
questions.explanation: If it replaces targeted support, the disabled and single parents may be worse off.

evidence.quote: could be left worse off

questions.text: What is his third objection based on?
options: The values of contribution and work
The cost of printing the money
Experience from other countries
The results of public opinion polls
questions.explanation: He says it is about values: work provides structure, belonging and contribution.

evidence.quote: Work gives people more than a wage.

questions.text: Why does he mention training, childcare and decent jobs?
options: To praise the present system of benefits
To ask for lower taxes on workers
To criticise the unemployed and their choices
To offer an alternative use of the money
questions.explanation: He says he would rather spend the money on those things, which respect people as participants.

evidence.quote: I would rather spend that money on training, on childcare and on decent jobs.

questions.text: What does Professor Lindqvist say about the trials overall?
options: They show less than either side claims
They prove that basic income fails in practice
They prove that basic income works in practice
They have never been run in any country
questions.explanation: He says the trials show rather less than either speaker would like.

evidence.quote: which is rather less than either would like

questions.text: What did recipients do with reduced working hours?
options: Started new companies of their own
Went on extended holidays abroad
Often studied or cared for relatives
Stopped paying rent to their landlords
questions.explanation: Those who reduced hours often used the time for study or care of relatives.

evidence.quote: used the time for study or care of relatives

questions.text: Why does he say temporary payments limit what we can conclude?
options: Recipients forgot about the money once the year ended
Temporary payments were too small to change behaviour
The trials were mostly paid for by higher taxes
People behave differently if they know the money will stop
questions.explanation: He says people behave differently when they know the money will stop.

evidence.quote: People behave differently when they know the money will stop

questions.text: What is his conclusion?
options: The trials settle the debate in favour of basic income
Evidence is irrelevant to a question of values
Basic income is unaffordable in every circumstance
The trials ease one fear but leave affordability open
questions.explanation: He says the trials rebut the crudest fear but cannot settle affordability.

evidence.quote: but they cannot settle the central question of affordability

questions.text: What is the effect of his final sentence?
options: To warn both sides against overstating the evidence
To oppose the motion on grounds of cost
To thank the speakers for their evidence
To support the motion on grounds of dignity
questions.explanation: He says anyone claiming the evidence proves their case is claiming more than it will bear.

evidence.quote: is claiming more than it will bear

questions.text: Why does Mai ask her question?
options: To support the motion with a personal story
To suggest a cheaper scheme for low earners
To challenge the fairness of who pays
To ask about the results of the trials
questions.explanation: She asks who pays and whether it is fair to tax a working nurse.

evidence.quote: who exactly pays?

questions.text: What does Peter's first comment suggest about Mai's question?
options: It was put with strong feeling
It was too long for the time allowed
It was off-topic for this stage of debate
It was meant as a joke by Mai
questions.explanation: He says the question has been put with some feeling.

evidence.quote: the question has been put with some feeling

questions.text: What does Mai say about her own position?
options: She works for the government on welfare policy
She is against the motion on grounds of cost
She has not yet made up her mind
She is in favour of the motion, with reservations
questions.explanation: She says she is undecided and would like to be persuaded.

evidence.quote: I'm actually undecided.

questions.text: What does Peter ask the audience to do when voting?
options: Judge the argument rather than the speaker
Vote for the speaker they like most
Abstain from voting if they remain undecided
Vote before the closing speeches have ended
questions.explanation: He invites them to vote on the argument, not on the speaker.

evidence.quote: vote on the argument, not on the speaker

questions.text: What worries Mai most?
options: The behaviour of the speakers in the debate
The length of the debate and its format
The date of the vote and the ballot
A large decision resting on small experiments
questions.explanation: She says something so large could be decided on the strength of small experiments.

evidence.quote: decided on the strength of small experiments
